messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
65,000 ft on one I205, single stage.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: the target is 65,000 ft. That is 65000 * 0.3048 = 19,800 m (about, within 5%). The motor is a single I205 (fixed) and the rocket is single stage (fixed). Nothing is said about landing speed, wind, rail or site, so I assume 6 m/s, 2 m/s of wind, a 1.5 m rail and sea level.
2. Feasibility: the no-drag speed for 19,800 m is sqrt(2*9.81*19800) = 623 m/s. An I motor carries only a few hundred newton-seconds, and drag at several hundred metres per second will throw away most of a vacuum coast. I still want the I205's real impulse before I decide the request cannot be met.

2. Feasibility: it comes back as the AeroTech HP-I205W, class I, 346.4 N*s, average thrust 204.4 N, burn 1.68 s. Case 0.029 m by 0.305 m, loaded 0.315 kg, propellant 0.188 kg, and the only delay is 14 s. A drag-free 0.40 kg rocket would leave burnout at 346.4 / 0.40 = 866 m/s and coast 866^2 / (2*9.81) = 38,200 m. That vacuum number clears 19,800 m, and it is not a flight anyone can fly. I will still run the lightest single-stage tube I can draw, so the gap is a tool result rather than a guess.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.45 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 204.4 / (0.45 * 9.81) = 46.3. Pad weight 0.45 * 9.81 = 4.41 N, acceleration on the rail (204.4 - 4.41) / 0.45 = 444 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 444 * 1.5) = 36.5 m/s. Descent mass 0.45 - 0.188 = 0.26 kg. Chute for 5 m/s: area 2 * 0.26 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.208 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.208 / 3.1416) = 0.51 m. I will use 0.55 m and open it at apogee, motor plugged, so the 14 s delay cannot cut the coast off early.
4. Draft: polystyrene ogive 0.10 m long on a 0.48 m cardboard tube, 0.038 m outside, 0.8 mm wall. Mount 0.033 m outside and 0.32 m long, HP-I205W plugged. Three balsa fins, root 0.10 m, tip 0.040 m, span 0.055 m, sweep 0.050 m, 3 mm thick. Chute 0.55 m at apogee. Default wind and rail.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the light single-stage rocket flies, and it does not come close to 65,000 ft. The simulator gives 1,664.4 m. That is 19800 / 1664.4 = 11.9 times below about 19,800 m, which is (19800 - 1664.4) / 19800 = 91.6% short. Margin is 1.31 cal at the rail and through the burn. Landing is 4.2 m/s, rail exit 43.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 52.0. The chute opens at 12.3 s, on the 12.33 s apogee. Mass is 0.4 kg. Mach 1.79 brings the supersonic-drag warning, which is the whole reason the vacuum coast does not happen.
5. Fix: nothing to change on this motor. 1,664.4 m still misses about 19,800 m, and a lighter nose or a smaller fin will not multiply the height by 12. One I205, single stage, is infeasible for 65,000 ft.
6. Uncertainty: the drag warning means 1,664.4 m could shift by hundreds of metres. It cannot shift by the missing 18 km. The impulse, 346.4 N*s, is the motor the database returned. The 0.55 m chute and a real build mass are what move the 4.2 m/s landing, not the altitude verdict.
messages.content:
Infeasible: one I205 cannot reach 65,000 ft in a single stage.
A plugged HP-I205W in a 38 mm cardboard rocket, the light build, reaches 1,664.4 m with 1.31 cal and lands at 4.2 m/s.
That is about 12 times short of 19,800 m. The flight is safe. The altitude is not available on this motor.
